name: Peptime
tagline: Real certificates from a named US lab that verify back to the lab, attached to an origin story the public record doesn't support.
summary: Peptime is better documented than an earlier read suggested, and worse corroborated. The testing is real: certificates are issued by Freedom Diagnostics in Franklin, Tennessee, and the retatrutide report shows 99.87% purity by HPLC-UV with identity confirmed by LC-MS. Two checks back that up, the certificate's accession appears in Freedom's public index of more than 56,000 records, and the file Peptime serves is byte-for-byte the lab's own, so nothing has been re-rendered in between. Finnrick adds genuine outside coverage: 10 tests, 8 passes, an 80% rating. The problems are elsewhere. BPC-157 rates 50% across four independent tests against a site-wide '>99% purity' claim. The certificates cover identity, purity and net content only, no sterility, heavy metals or endotoxin, and none of them can be browsed to; you have to already know the URL. And the marketed history does not hold: the site claims 14+ years and compounding since 2012, but peptime.com served a placeholder page at every archived capture from 2010 until mid-2025, the operating entity was formed in Delaware in March 2026, and the storefront first appears in May 2026.
differentiator: One of the few vendors whose certificates can be checked twice over, traced back to the issuing lab's own public index, and byte-compared against the lab's original file.
standoutPro: The largest peptide-brand presence on X in this catalog by roughly 100x, 7,820 followers against a next-best 62, backed by certificates from a named US laboratory that verify independently: the accession resolves in Freedom Diagnostics' public 56,000-record index and the served file is MD5-identical to the lab's own.
standoutCon: The marketed 14-year history is contradicted by the archive record, which shows a parked domain until 2025 and a company formed in 2026. BPC-157 rates 50% independently against a >99% purity claim, the panel omits all contaminant testing, and no certificate can be found without guessing its URL.
verdict: The lab work is legitimate and checkable, which is more than most vendors offer. The history around it is not, and BPC-157 is an unresolved quality problem. Buy on the batch certificate, not the brand story.

name: One Aminos
location: Ships from Washington, D.C.; manufacturing stated as Florida
tagline: A full seven-assay panel from a named laboratory, and certificates that verify back to that lab's own database.
summary: One Aminos publishes more panel coverage than most vendors twice its size, and it is not self-reported. Every batch is tested by United Laboratories, a pharmaceutical analytical lab in Punjab, India, whose director signs each report; the certificates name One Aminos LLC as the client and cover identity by LC-MS, purity by RP-HPLC, net content, conformity across three individually-assayed vials, sterility, heavy metals by ICP-MS, and bacterial endotoxin by kinetic chromogenic LAL. Reported purity runs 99.3% and up. Crucially, each report carries a verification code that resolves against the laboratory's own records, we checked one and the lab confirmed the product, batch, strength and issue date. What is still missing is outside scrutiny. Every test so far is one the vendor commissioned; no independent surveillance testing exists on Finnrick or Disclosed Labs, the laboratory claims no ISO 17025 accreditation, and its sterility result is described on the certificate as a preliminary screen rather than full compendial testing. The storefront is also about a month old.
differentiator: Publishes a complete seven-assay panel per batch from day one, and, unusually, certificates a buyer can verify directly with the issuing laboratory rather than take on trust.
standoutPro: A named laboratory, a full seven-assay panel including sterility, heavy metals and endotoxin, three vials assayed per batch, and certificates that verify back to the lab's own database, the paperwork here is checkable, which most vendors' is not.
standoutCon: All of it is testing the vendor paid for. No independent surveillance record exists anywhere, the laboratory claims no ISO 17025 accreditation, its sterility result is explicitly a preliminary screen, and the storefront is about a month old with no review history and no named principal.
verdict: The disclosure format is right, the panel is complete, and the certificates hold up when you check them with the lab. The remaining gap is that nobody outside this arrangement has tested the product yet, that, and time, are what would move it.

verdict: The certificates are worth reading and the prices are easy to check, which is more than most anonymous storefronts offer. Treat the lot documents as the whole of the evidence, because there is nothing behind them.

summary: Vril presents as an EU brand with proprietary supply. It is a dropship rebrand of aipeptidetech.com / HK Qiangtai, and its own paperwork gives it away: the certificates it hosts are redacted in the Client and Manufacturer fields, but the QR code printed on each one resolves to the public Janoshik record serving the unredacted original naming the actual supplier. The operator confirmed the redaction is intentional. On 2026-05-21 the brand publicly admitted shipping directly from China, contradicting its own supplier claim. Separately, the founder account has a documented history of token-promotion pitches and of dumping partnered DeSci token positions. The product itself may well be real, a Janoshik-tested retatrutide batch returned 99.886% purity, but everything around it is misrepresented.
differentiator: Included as a worked example of what a misrepresenting vendor looks like, not as a purchase option.
standoutPro: The one defensible positive: a Janoshik-tested retatrutide batch returned 99.886% purity, so the product appears to be genuine.
standoutCon: Structured misrepresentation, deliberately redacted certificates that are not even the brand's own tests, a public admission that contradicts its supplier claim, and a founder account with documented token-dumping behavior.
verdict: The chemistry may be fine; the representation is not. Listed as a case study in what to look for, and the only F-tier vendor carrying no discount code.
